messages.subject: Loading multiple files into R on a Mac
messages.subject_clean: Loading multiple files into R on a Mac
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I'm right now working through chapter 4 of QCLWR on my Mac and sometimes have problems with loading and saving files as described in the code.
Just now I was trying to load the two files "corp_bnc_sgml_2.txt" and "corp_bnc_sgml_4.txt" into R in order to create a frequency list of them. I hope that I didn't misunderstand the task!

 I first tried doing this with the following (due to the 2nd grey box on p. 114):

> corpus.files<-file.choose() # I understand that this is the Mac function for choose.files()

Unfortunately this only allows to select one file (as I also found confirmed in this previous post: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/corpling-with-r/load$20several$20files/corpling-with-r/7iVCm34lAbM/7-8uz6SekQIJ)

Then I looked at the all code file and it contained a select.list function for Mac/Linux users, which I copied and pasted. Here is the output:

 > corpus.files<-select.list(dir(scan(nmax=1, what="char")), multiple=T)
1: /Users/violawiegand/_qclwr/_inputfiles/corp_bnc_sgml_2.txt
Read 1 item

:

Enter one or more numbers separated by spaces, or an empty line to cancel
1:
> corpus.files
character(0)

I had expected a dialogue to pop up, similarly to file.choose() so that I could choose the two files. This was not the case and instead I tried entering one of the file names upon the "1:" prompt. However, this didn't seem to work, as corpus.files doesn't seem to contain the contents of corp_bnc_sgml_2.txt. How should I react to this prompt properly? Or is there any other way that I could choose multiple files on a Mac?

Thank you!

Best,
Viola

messages.subject: Scanning text file warning message: "embedded nul(s) found in input"
messages.subject_clean: Scanning text file warning message: "embedded nul(s) found in input"
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I am trying to generate a frequency list of my own corpus. When I applied the QCLWR instructions on generating a frequency list of an unannotated corpus (p. 106 following) to my own data the following warning message was returned:

> textfile<-scan(file.choose(), what="char", sep="\n", quote="", comment.char="")
Read 69745 items
Warning message:
In scan(file.choose(), what = "char", sep = "\n", quote = "", comment.char = "") :
  embedded nul(s) found in input

Does anyone know what the 'embedded nul(s)' mean and whether they imply that there's a serious problem with my data?

I had merged all text files into one file using the mac command line (cat [file names] -> all-merged.txt) , is it possible that something went wrong and corrupted the data?

Thanks!

Best,
Viola

Has anyone ever used FRANTEXT and tried to import concordance hits (or even the sub-corpora, which would be a breakthrough) into R?

Many thanks,

C. Bechet

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] How to download corpus data from online electronic sources like FRANTEXT?
messages.subject_clean: [CorpLing with R] How to download corpus data from online electronic sources like FRANTEXT?
messages.body_plain:
I've successfully used RCurl <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RCurl/index.html> to write several R scripts that log into the Corpus of Contemporary American English <http://corpus.byu.edu/coca/> and the Corpus del Español <http://www.corpusdelespanol.org/> in order to retrieve concordance lines and frequency numbers of words and strings:

https://github.com/ekbrown/Rscripts/blob/master/Script_search_COCA_ekb.R
https://github.com/ekbrown/Rscripts/blob/master/Script_freq_COCA_ekb.R
https://github.com/ekbrown/Rscripts/blob/master/Script_search_CdE_ekb.R
https://github.com/ekbrown/Rscripts/blob/master/Script_freq_CdE_ekb.R

However, if I were to write those scripts from scratch today, I'd use httr <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/httr/index.html>, which is a user-friendly interface to curl <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/curl/index.html>, another R package (in addition to RCurl) that is built on the C library libcurl <http://curl.haxx.se/libcurl/>.

For (static) webpages that don't require authentication, the scan() function, as described in QCLWR, is great.

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] How to download corpus data from online electronic sources like FRANTEXT?
messages.subject_clean: [CorpLing with R] How to download corpus data from online electronic sources like FRANTEXT?
messages.body_plain:
If you change the "html" to "txt" in the URL, that is:

http://www.gutenberg.org/robot/harvest?filetypes[]=txt&langs[]=nl

the zipped files will contain .txt files rather than .htm files, which will be easier to deal with. Afterwards, you can use:

library("readr")
read_lines("file_name.zip")

to read in the zipped files without having to manually unzip them, as readr::read_lines() can read in zipped files directly into R.

You might approach it like this:

install.packages("rvest")
install.packages("readr")
install.packages("textcat")

# gets links on first page
library("rvest")
links.to.zipped.files <-
  html("http://www.gutenberg.org/robot/harvest?filetypes[]=txt&langs[]=nl") %>%
  html_nodes("a") %>%
  html_attr("href") %>%
  grep("\\.zip$", ., value = TRUE)
  # grep("[^-8]\\.zip$", ., value = TRUE)  # if the "-8.zip" and ".zip" files are the same, use this line instead of the previous one

# downloads zipped files to a new directory
dir.create("Dutch_novels")
setwd("Dutch_novels")
for (i in links.to.zipped.files[1:3]) {
  download.file(url = i, destfile = basename(i))
}

# loads zipped files
library("readr")
library("textcat")
file.names <- list.files()
for (i in file.names) {

  cur.file <- read_lines(i)

  # limits to Dutch lines
  # *** use this with caution, as it's not very accurate ***
  langs <- textcat(cur.file)
  cur.file <- cur.file[grep("dutch", langs)]

  ### more cleaning up and processing as needed

}

If you want to get more than the links on the first page you'll need to get the "Next Page" link at the bottom of the page with something like this:

link.to.next.page <http://link.to.next.page> <-
  html("http://www.gutenberg.org/robot/harvest?filetypes[]=txt&langs[]=nl") %>%
  html_nodes("a") %>%
  html_attr("href") %>%
  grep("offset=\\d+", ., value = T) %>%
  paste0("http://www.gutenberg.org/robot/", .)

And then you can loop over the "Next Page" links until you have as many links as you want, following the logic in Stefan's assignments about the web:

http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/research/qclwr/other_3.pdf
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/research/qclwr/other_4.pdf
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/research/qclwr/other_5.pdf

Best of luck.

messages.subject_clean: Question about collostructional analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm also having hard time doing collostructional analysis. I'm using a 573,987 word corpus of historical Dutch which is not annotated. I would like to use colexeme analysis in order to determine which verbs in a given slot are most strongly attracted to a grammatical construction, nl. "instead of" (its Dutch counterpart). Here follows the configuration of my construction:

[Subject VERB X instead of Y] (e.g. "I'm wearing the red shirt instead of the blue one").

For coll. analysis, I need the following:

- the name of the construction I wish to study ("instead of"); ==> OK
- the frequency of all elements that could potentially occur in the construction, nl. all verbs (tokens) that occur in the corpus; ==> PROBLEMATIC!
- the combined frequency of all construction tokens (in my case: 24); ==> OK
- A table with the three columns ‘VERB’, ‘corpus_frequency ’, and ‘construction_frequency’. ==> OK

The second element that is needed can hardly be obtained since the corpus is not tagged for POS. Does it mean that coll. analysis can only be used with annotated corpora, or is there another alternative to coll. analysis?

Best regards,

C. Bechet

Le jeudi 25 avril 2013 19:04:24 UTC+2, MatíasG a écrit :
> Hi everyone,
>
> I'm having some hard time doing collostructional analysis with a corpus. If I follow the methods outlined here: http://www-user.uni-bremen.de/~anatol/crs/caw/sclx.html The test indicates that some how almost all lemas are used significantly more often with the anallysed construction than expected. However, if I instead of using number of other lemas of the same type in the construction and related constructions, I use the number of sentences for the construction and related constructions, I get sensible results.
>
> Why is this procedure with counts of sentences wrong? What might it be that I'm doing wrong?
>
> Thanks a lot,
>
> Matías

Yes, that is the biggest issue. Complex prepositions are hard to study in a quantitative approach, as far as diachrony is concerned. Sometimes examples are scarce in historical corpora. In a corpora of present day Dutch, for instance, there are more than 40,000 instances of the construction "in plaats van", against only 27 for "in stede van". How could I compare collocational preferences for each construction in order to find significant semantic differences between them? Distinctive collexem analysis seemed the best option at first glance...

Yes, that is the biggest issue. Complex prepositions are hard to study in a quantitative approach, as far as diachrony is concerned. Sometimes examples are scarce in historical corpora. In a corpus of present day Dutch, for instance, there are more than 40,000 instances of the construction "in plaats van", against only 27 for "in stede van". How could I compare collocational preferences for each construction in order to find significant semantic differences between them? Distinctive collexeme analysis seemed the best option at first sight...

messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am attempting a collexeme analysis of the abstract nouns occurring in the Det-N pattern in a few small corpora. I have two questions:

ONE: As I understand it, typically what is loaded in the txt file is a table that lists every word under analysis occurring in the corpus (in my case, singular nouns), their frequency in the collostruction, and their frequency in the corpus.

I first tried this only including the 50 most frequent words occurring in the Det-N pattern (there were 1577 total). Then I realized maybe I would not then be able to detect repulsion strengths because I didn't include all nouns, even those not occurring in the pattern. Also, maybe I would still see strong word/structure strength among those words occurring just a few times in the corpus so I should include them. Finally, and perhaps this is most important, the program prompts me for the number of Det-N occurrences in the corpus. I entered the total number of Det-N occurrences (1577), and then when uploading the table file only included those 50 mentioned earlier. Would this impact the results, since those remaining Det-N occurrences weren't to be found in the table I uploaded? I hope this question is clear, and I thank you for any advice!

TWO: Would you recommend I include all Det-N occurrences (not just those with an abstract noun) in my table? Maybe I should, since it would perhaps better reveal the degree to which the pattern "favors" abstract nouns as opposed to others (e.g. book, year, etc.).

I appreciate your time,
Brian

> ONE: As I understand it, typically what is loaded in the txt file is a table that lists every word under analysis occurring in the corpus (in my case, singular nouns), their frequency in the collostruction, and their frequency in the corpus.

Correct.

> I first tried this only including the 50 most frequent words occurring in the Det-N pattern (there were 1577 total). Then I realized maybe I would not then be able to detect repulsion strengths because I didn't include all nouns, even those not occurring in the pattern.

Yes, for repulsion, you would need to include the low-frequency items
as well. Repulsion approximations for unattested items will be
provided at the bottom of the results.

> most important, the program prompts me for the number of Det-N occurrences in the corpus. I entered the total number of Det-N occurrences (1577), and then when uploading the table file only included those 50 mentioned earlier. Would this impact the results

It shouldn't impact the results for the 50 included, no.

> TWO: Would you recommend I include all Det-N occurrences (not just those with an abstract noun) in my table?

Yes.

STG
